sentences.text: The name Pterodactylus translates to 'winged finger' and refers to a genus of extinct pterosaurs.
This animal was a small pterosaur that lived earlier than the Late Cretaceous genera Pteranodon and Quetzalcoatlus.
The adult Pterodactylus antiquus had an estimated wingspan of about 1.04 meters based on an isolated skull.
Adult skulls were long and thin, containing approximately 90 narrow and conical teeth.
The flying monsters ridden by the Nazgûl in J.R.R. Tolkien's legendarium were described as looking similarly built to Pterodactylus.
The informal term 'pterodactyl' is often mistakenly used to refer to any pterosaur, but specifically applies to Pterodactylus and the unrelated Pteranodon.
Pterodactylus is popularly known for its elongated head crest and large wings.
The first Pterodactylus specimen was described by Cosimo Alessandro Collini in 1784 from fossils found in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria.
The type species of the genus is Ornithocephalus antiquus.
In 1846, Hermann von Meyer described the species Pterodactylus gemmingi, a name honoring fossil collector Carl Eming von Gemming.
Pterodactylus was a generalist carnivore that likely ate a variety of invertebrates and vertebrates.
It was a carnivore that likely hunted fish and other small animals.
Youngest immature P. antiquus specimens had as few as 15 teeth with relatively broad bases.
Other P. antiquus specimens had narrower and more numerous teeth, up to 90 in some cases.
A third year class of P. antiquus specimens, including some large ones once assigned to P. kochi, all show signs of immaturity.
Distinct year classes in P. antiquus fossils suggest the species bred seasonally and grew consistently throughout its life.
The smallest size class of P. antiquus likely consisted of individuals less than one year old that had just begun to fly.
The second year class of P. antiquus represented individuals one to two years old, while the rare third year class included specimens over two years old.
Comparisons of scleral rings suggest P. antiquus may have been diurnal.
Comparisons of scleral ring patterns suggest Pterodactylus antiquus may have been diurnal.
The genus Pterodactylus was originally placed under the authority of Bonaparte in 1838.
Over its 200-year history, Pterodactylus has undergone numerous classification changes, resulting in many synonyms.
Revisions by Peter Wellnhofer in the 1980s reduced the number of recognized Pterodactylus species to about six.
By the early 21st century, Pterodactylus antiquus and P. kochi were the only well-known and well-supported species remaining.
Fossils of Pterodactylus are primarily found in the Solnhofen limestone of Bavaria, Germany, dating from the Late Jurassic Tithonian stage between 150.8 and 148.5 million years ago.
Fossils of Pterodactylus date to the Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic.
The Solnhofen Limestone is a diverse fossil site containing detailed imprints of soft-bodied organisms like jellyfishes.
In 1996, Christopher Bennett suggested that differences between Pterodactylus kochi and P. antiquus were due to age differences, making them the same species.
It is debated whether Pterodactylus possessed a bony crest or a soft-tissue crest, with some studies suggesting it may lack a bony cranial crest entirely.
It is debated whether fully adult Pterodactylus specimens are unknown or were mistakenly classified as other genera.
